The reason I compared holding TI to holding Coca-Cola is that… while browsing the web yesterday, I came across an article about a legendary portfolio manager who held TI for over 30 years and earned enormous returns.

This is a really interesting chart.
I attended the TrendForce San Francisco roadshow yesterday, and this chart got me thinking about a lot of things.

China is now expected to localize more than half, or close to half, of most equipment categories, excluding lithography and track.
What does this mean? It means China can now expand mature node capacity far more easily than before, using equipment made domestically within China.

Mature node foundries are booming right now, right? That's thanks to the AI supercycle driving demand for PMICs, power semiconductors, and so on.

Samsung and TSMC shutting down their mature node capacity has also helped a lot.
But here's what I imagine... that China could oversupply mature foundry capacity.

Think about it. If China can be self sufficient in equipment, there's no limit to how far it can expand capacity. Then are companies like TI, with large revenue exposure to China, really safe?

I think it's time to take another look at Western mature foundry companies with a high share of China revenue.

Of course, I'm not saying sell TI right now. I'm just saying we should think about whether it makes sense to hold them for 10 years or more, like Coca Cola.

If you have a different view, please feel free to share it. I’d love to learn.

the real risk is if they stop getting contract-backed loans and have to borrow at that 15%.

say they need $20B more. at the ~6-9% they’ve been getting, that’s around $1.3-1.8B a year in interest. at 15% it’s $3B a year.

for context, they paid $640M in interest last quarter, so about $2.6B a year on everything they owe right now. one new $20B chunk at 15% would cost more than all of that. and they’re still not profitable.

the next financing deal is critical. if it’s contract-backed at single digits, fine. if they’re forced into 15% bonds, that’s when it gets really risky.

$CRWV isn’t paying 15% interest. Only 4% of their debt costs that.

I went through the Q2 10-Q line by line. Out of ~$35B in debt, exactly one loan sits at 15%. It’s $1.3B, due March 2028, and already being paid down.

The 15% chart going around is the market yield on their 2032 bond. A higher yield doesn’t change what CoreWeave pays. It works like a mortgage. If you locked in at 3% and rates go to 7%, you’re still paying 3%. CoreWeave locked that bond at 9.625% and still pays 9.625%.

What they actually pay

> $6.6B of convertibles at ~2%
> ~$10B of bonds at 9-10%
> Most secured loans around 9%
> ~8.4% blended across everything

They have roughly $20B of 2026 capex left to fund, and 2027 will need more. Their main funding tool has been loans backed by customer contracts. The investment grade one backed by Meta priced around 5.9% in March. If they keep borrowing that way, I think the math holds.

DeepSeek is back at it again.

Diving deeper, this happened on a Saturday, no less, so the markets haven't had time to react. Only the weekend perps have.

The headline driving it is DeepSeek's claim that the new model needs 4x less memory per token. 

That reads like less memory demand, until you look at the rest of the release:

+ The model is still huge. It has 552B parameters, and all of them have to sit in memory to run, even though only a fraction is active at a time.

+ It handles 1M tokens of context. Longer context means more memory per user.
+ It's priced at about $1.20 per million output tokens. Cheaper tokens have always meant more tokens used.

+ DeepSeek ran out of compute this week. It had a five-hour outage that experts blamed on not having enough capacity. A company that keeps making its models leaner and still can't keep its service up is evidence that demand is ahead of supply.

The weekend market has mostly recovered so far, so expect some reaction at Monday's open, but I wouldn't be surprised if the market shrugs it off by 10am.

Samsung and SK Hynix are both down more than 50% from their June highs, and they now trade at 2–3x their 2027–28 earnings.

In every previous memory upcycle (2001, 2008, 2018, 2022), the low end for these two was 4–7x. Their price-to-book is now near 1x, a level that usually shows up only at the bottom of a real bust, with warehouses full of unsold chips, DRAM prices cut in half and quarterly losses.

None of that is happening this time. 

Memory inventories at both companies fell below 10 days in September, and KB Securities has their earnings staying near record highs through 2028, with only a single-digit dip that year.

Every new generation of GPUs and custom chips also needs new memory: HBM, SOCAMM, LPDDR5 and enterprise SSDs. As the installed base gets refreshed, each upgrade cycle turns into another round of orders.

The market is pricing in a bust but the demand is ever increasing.

The selloff continues. Next, I’m shifting from shorting beta to shorting alpha. I call it the “reverse bottleneck trade”—the counterpart to the earlier bottleneck trade.

The logic is simple: AI demand will keep growing, but that growth may slow, while upstream suppliers keep expanding capacity in response to shortages and fat margins. Once effective supply catches up with demand, bargaining power shifts back downstream. During a shortage, customers care first about availability. Good enough will do. Once supply is plentiful, they start comparing performance, cost, power consumption, and reliability again. That’s when we find out who wins orders on competitiveness and who was simply picking up overflow because the leaders couldn’t supply enough.

My watchlist includes memory runner-up MU, second- and third-tier optical players COHR and AAOI, and foundry runner-up INTC.

This trade doesn’t even require the AI bubble to burst. Supply growth just needs to start outpacing demand growth. I think there’s a very high probability these stocks put in an “Everest chart” over the next year—a towering peak followed by a collapse back down. If you don’t have the stomach to go all-in on outright shorts, anti-bottleneck pair trades are another good way to express the view: long LITE / short AAOI; long TSM / short INTC; long NVDA / short AMD or AVGO.
